source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 8 (PDF 167-188, printed 167-188); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 8 (Chemical Equilibrium), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Macroscopic events are those phenomena which:

options.text: can be seen only with an electron microscope
involve only the breaking of bonds
can be observed with the naked eye

blocks.explanation: Macroscopic events can be observed with the naked eye without considering the individual particles (8.1.1).

book_ref.quote: phenomena that can be observed with the naked eye without considering the individual particles

blocks.prompt: 2 Which one of the following is a macroscopic property of a reaction?
blocks.explanation: Formation of a precipitate can be seen; the other three are microscopic events (8.1.1, 8.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Change in colour, the evolution or absorption of heat, the formation of precipitate

blocks.prompt: 3 Which of the following is a microscopic event?
blocks.explanation: Breaking and forming bonds cannot be seen with the naked eye, so it is a microscopic event (8.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The collisions between molecules, breaking and forming bonds, rearrangement of atoms

blocks.prompt: 4 An irreversible reaction stops when:

options.text: the rates of forward and reverse reactions become equal
the limiting reactant is used up

blocks.explanation: In an irreversible reaction the reactants are completely consumed; it stops when the limiting reactant is used up (8.1).

book_ref.quote: Such reactions stop when the limiting reactant is used up.

blocks.prompt: 5 At chemical equilibrium, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are:
blocks.explanation: At equilibrium the concentrations become constant and the forward and reverse rates become equal (8.1).

book_ref.quote: At this point, the concentrations of reactants and products become constant

blocks.prompt: 6 In the equation PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), the double arrow shows that the reaction is:
blocks.explanation: The double arrow tells that the reaction is reversible (8.1).

book_ref.quote: The double arrow tells that the reaction is reversible.

blocks.prompt: 7 A reversible reaction reaches chemical equilibrium when it is carried out in a container which:

options.text: prevents the entry or escape of any substance
allows only the reactants to enter

blocks.explanation: Equilibrium is reached in a container which prevents the entry or escape of any substance involved (8.1).

book_ref.quote: in a container which prevents the entry or escape of any of the substances involved

blocks.text: 8.2 Reversible reactions, microscopic events and dynamic equilibrium

blocks.prompt: 8 When steam and carbon monoxide are mixed, the forward reaction has its maximum rate:
blocks.explanation: At the start the number of collisions per second between H₂O and CO is maximum, so the forward rate is maximum at the beginning (8.2).

book_ref.quote: Therefore, the forward reaction has its maximum rate at the beginning.

blocks.prompt: 9 In the reaction H₂O(g) + CO(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + CO₂(g), the products formed are:
blocks.explanation: Bonds in CO and H₂O break and new bonds form to produce H₂ and CO₂ (8.2).

book_ref.quote: As H₂O and CO are gradually used up, the forward reaction slows down.

blocks.prompt: 10 At the start of the reaction between steam and CO, the rate of the reverse reaction is:

options.text: low, then increases and finally becomes constant
equal to the forward rate from the start

blocks.explanation: At the start the reverse rate is low, gradually increases as H₂ and CO₂ accumulate, and finally becomes constant (8.2).

book_ref.quote: at the start, the rate of the reverse reaction is low, gradually increases, and finally becomes constant

blocks.prompt: 11 At the state of chemical equilibrium:

options.text: all the reactants have been used up
the composition of the mixture does not change

blocks.explanation: At chemical equilibrium the composition of the reaction mixture does not change and the forward and reverse rates are equal (8.2).

book_ref.quote: composition of the reaction mixture does not change and forward and reverse rates are equal

blocks.prompt: 12 For the general reaction A ⇌ B, at the equilibrium position the concentration of A compared with that of B:

options.text: may be equal, lower or greater

blocks.explanation: Figure 8.1 shows that at equilibrium the reactant and product may be equal, or the reactant may be lower or greater than the product (8.2).

book_ref.quote: the concentrations of the reactant and the product may be equal as shown in Figure 8.1 (a)

blocks.prompt: 13 In all the concentration-time graphs of Figure 8.1, after equilibrium is established the concentrations:
blocks.explanation: For all the graphs, after equilibrium is established the concentrations become constant (8.2).

book_ref.quote: for all of these graphs, it is clear that after the equilibrium is established, the concentrations become constant

blocks.prompt: 14 Chemical equilibrium is called dynamic because:

options.text: molecules keep reacting in both directions at equal rates

blocks.explanation: Individual molecules constantly react, but the forward and reverse rates are the same, so the equilibrium is dynamic (8.2).

book_ref.quote: The system is dynamic because the individual molecules are constantly reacting

blocks.text: 8.3 Relation between macroscopic and microscopic events

blocks.prompt: 15 Macroscopic events are the result of:

options.text: only the use of a catalyst

blocks.explanation: Macroscopic events are the result of multiple simultaneous microscopic events (8.3).

book_ref.quote: Macroscopic events are the result of multiple simultaneous microscopic events.

blocks.prompt: 16 The rates of the forward and reverse reactions in an equilibrium system are affected by:

options.text: the colour of the container only
the size of the container label

blocks.explanation: Collisions change the forward and reverse rates, which are affected by activation energy and external factors (8.3).

book_ref.quote: These collisions change the rates of forward and reverse reactions

blocks.prompt: 17 The escape of liquid molecules from the surface into the gaseous phase in a closed container is called:
blocks.explanation: Molecules near the surface with enough energy escape into the gas phase; this is evaporation (8.3).

book_ref.quote: some of the liquid molecules near the surface have enough energy to escape into the gaseous phase

blocks.prompt: 18 Vapour molecules colliding with the liquid surface and being captured again by the liquid is called:
blocks.explanation: Vapour molecules captured again by the liquid surface show condensation (8.3).

book_ref.quote: molecules in vapour phase can also collide with the liquid surface and be captured again by the liquid

blocks.prompt: 19 When a liquid and its vapour are at dynamic equilibrium in a closed container:

options.text: the rates of evaporation and condensation are equal

blocks.explanation: At dynamic equilibrium evaporation and condensation occur at equal rates and the vapour pressure stays constant at a given temperature (8.3).

book_ref.quote: At dynamic equilibrium, the vapor pressure remains constant at a given temperature

blocks.prompt: 20 When the temperature of a liquid in equilibrium with its vapour is raised, the system reaches a new equilibrium with:
blocks.explanation: Higher temperature raises the average kinetic energy and the evaporation rate, so the new equilibrium has a higher vapour pressure (8.3).

book_ref.quote: Finally, the system will reach a new state of dynamic equilibrium, with a higher equilibrium vapor pressure.

blocks.text: 8.4 Dynamic equilibrium between two physical states

blocks.prompt: 21 In a dynamic equilibrium:

options.text: changes continue but no net change is observed

blocks.explanation: Although continuous changes take place, no net change in the system as a whole is observed (8.4).

book_ref.quote: no net change in the system as a whole is observed

blocks.prompt: 22 Ice and water coexist in dynamic equilibrium at:
blocks.explanation: At 0 °C ice and water coexist; water changes into ice and ice into water at the same rate (8.4).

book_ref.quote: For example, at 0 °C, ice and water coexist in equilibrium.

blocks.prompt: 23 The state of equilibrium applies only to:
blocks.explanation: The state of equilibrium only applies to reversible reactions (8.5).

book_ref.quote: The state of equilibrium only applies to reversible reactions.

blocks.prompt: 24 Equilibrium cannot be established when calcium carbonate is heated in an open vessel because:

options.text: the reaction is not reversible at all
a product escapes from the vessel

blocks.explanation: Equilibrium needs a closed vessel; no part of the reactants and products may escape. In an open vessel CO₂ escapes (8.5).

book_ref.quote: The equilibrium can be established only if the reaction vessel is closed.

blocks.prompt: 25 The state of equilibrium in a reversible reaction can be approached:

options.text: from either side, starting with reactants or products

blocks.explanation: Equilibrium can be approached from either side, whether we start with reactants or products (8.6).

book_ref.quote: can be approached from either side whether we start with reactants or products

blocks.prompt: 26 The value of the equilibrium constant of a reaction depends on:
blocks.explanation: Kc does not depend on initial concentrations; it is constant and depends on temperature only (8.6).

book_ref.quote: rather it is constants and depends on temperature only

blocks.prompt: 27 A catalyst added to a reversible reaction:

options.text: shifts the equilibrium to the right

blocks.explanation: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or constant; it helps to attain equilibrium earlier (8.6).

book_ref.quote: It helps to attain the equilibrium earlier.

blocks.prompt: 28 For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), the equilibrium constant expression is:
blocks.explanation: Pure solids are not included in the Kc expression, so only CO₂(g) appears: Kc = [CO₂] (8.6).

book_ref.quote: their concentrations are not included in the equilibrium constant expression

blocks.prompt: 29 With respect to the physical states of reactants and products, chemical equilibrium is of:
blocks.explanation: With respect to physical states there are two types: homogeneous and heterogeneous (8.7).

book_ref.quote: With respect to the physical states of reactants and products, there are two types

blocks.prompt: 30 An equilibrium in which all reactants and products are in the same phase is called:
blocks.explanation: When all the reactants and products are in the same phase, the equilibrium is homogeneous (8.7.1).

book_ref.quote: An equilibrium system in which all of the reactants and products are in the same phase.

blocks.prompt: 31 Which of the following is a homogeneous equilibrium?
blocks.explanation: In 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ every substance is a gas, so it is homogeneous; the others have solids and gases (8.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The following are examples of homogeneous equilibria:

blocks.prompt: 32 A heterogeneous equilibrium is one in which the reactants and products are:
blocks.explanation: In a heterogeneous equilibrium the reactants and products are in more than one phase (8.7).

book_ref.quote: An equilibrium in which the reactants and products are in more than one phases

blocks.prompt: 33 Which of these is an example of heterogeneous equilibrium?
blocks.explanation: Iron and Fe₃O₄ are solids while H₂O and H₂ are gases: more than one phase (8.7).

book_ref.quote: The following are examples of heterogeneous equilibrium:

blocks.prompt: 34 For C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g), the equilibrium constant expression is:
blocks.explanation: Solid carbon is left out of the expression (Keep in Mind, 8.6), so Kc = [CO][H₂]/[H₂O] (8.7).

book_ref.quote: The following are examples of heterogeneous equilibrium:

blocks.prompt: 35 The esterification CH₃COOH(l) + C₂H₅OH(l) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) + H₂O(l) is a homogeneous equilibrium because:

options.text: all the substances are in the liquid phase
the products are in a different phase

blocks.explanation: All four substances are in the same (liquid) phase, so the equilibrium is homogeneous (8.7.1).

book_ref.quote: The following are examples of homogeneous equilibria:

blocks.text: 8.8 Equilibrium constant and position of equilibrium

blocks.prompt: 36 The relation between equilibrium concentrations that leads to the equilibrium constant was discovered in 1864 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1864 the Norwegian chemists C. Guldberg and P. Waage measured many equilibrium compositions and found the constant ratio (8.8).

book_ref.quote: In 1864, the Norwegian chemists C. Guldberg (1836–1902) and P. Waage (1833–1900)

blocks.prompt: 37 In the law of mass action, the term 'active mass' means:
blocks.explanation: By active mass we mean the molar concentration, expressed in moles dm⁻³ (8.8).

book_ref.quote: By the term active mass, we mean the molar concentration.

blocks.prompt: 38 In an equilibrium constant expression, square brackets [ ] stand for:
blocks.explanation: Molar concentration, in moles dm⁻³, is expressed by square brackets [ ] (8.8).

book_ref.quote: This concentration is expressed by square brackets [ ].

blocks.prompt: 39 According to the law of mass action, the rate of a reaction is directly proportional to:

options.text: the active masses of the reactants raised to their coefficients

blocks.explanation: The rate is directly proportional to the active masses of the reactants, raised to the coefficients in the balanced equation (8.8).

book_ref.quote: The rate of the chemical reaction is directly proportional to the active masses of the reactants

blocks.prompt: 40 In terms of the forward rate constant kf and the reverse rate constant kr, Kc is equal to:
blocks.explanation: At equilibrium kf[A][B] = kr[C][D], so kf/kr = [C][D]/[A][B] = Kc (8.8).

book_ref.quote: The left side of this equation is the ratio of two rate constants

blocks.prompt: 41 For a reversible reaction the forward rate constant is 6.0 × 10⁻³ and the reverse rate constant is 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ (same units). Kc is:

book_ref.quote: The left side of this equation is the ratio of two rate constants

blocks.prompt: 42 For A + B ⇌ C + D, the rate of the forward reaction is written as:
blocks.explanation: By the law of mass action, rate of forward reaction ∝ [A][B] = kf[A][B] (8.8).

book_ref.quote: ‘kf’ is the proportionality constant, and is known as forward rate constant.

blocks.prompt: 43 For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), the equilibrium constant expression is:
blocks.explanation: Each concentration is raised to its coefficient: Kc = [NH₃]²/[N₂][H₂]³ (8.8.1).

book_ref.quote: where a, b, c and d are the coefficients of balanced equation.

blocks.prompt: 44 For 2N₂O₅(g) ⇌ 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), the equilibrium constant expression is:
blocks.explanation: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: Kc = [NO₂]⁴[O₂]/[N₂O₅]² (8.8.1).

book_ref.quote: This equation is known as equilibrium constant expression.

blocks.prompt: 45 An esterification mixture of 250 cm³ at equilibrium contains 0.100 mol ethanoic acid, 0.050 mol ethanol, 0.200 mol ethyl ethanoate and 0.100 mol water. Kc is:
blocks.explanation: Concentrations: acid 0.400, ethanol 0.200, ester 0.800, water 0.400 mol dm⁻³. Kc = (0.800 × 0.400)/(0.400 × 0.200) = 4.0, no units (8.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Use this data to calculate a value of Kc for this reaction.

blocks.prompt: 46 A mixture of 0.0600 mol dm⁻³ propanone and 0.0600 mol dm⁻³ HCN reaches equilibrium with 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ of product. The equilibrium concentration of propanone is:
blocks.explanation: 1 mol of propanone is used per mole of product: 0.0600 − 0.0200 = 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ (8.8.1).

book_ref.quote: A mixture of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ propanone and 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ hydrogen cyanide is left to reach equilibrium

blocks.prompt: 47 Using the data of the previous question (propanone and HCN each 0.0400 mol dm⁻³, product 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ at equilibrium), Kc is:
blocks.explanation: Kc = 0.0200/(0.0400 × 0.0400) = 12.5; the unit is (mol dm⁻³)⁻¹ = mol⁻¹ dm³ (8.8.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: A mixture of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ propanone and 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ hydrogen cyanide is left to reach equilibrium

blocks.prompt: 48 Kc has no units when:

options.text: the moles of reactants and products in the balanced equation are equal

blocks.explanation: When the moles of reactants and products in the balanced equation are equal, the units cancel (8.8.2).

book_ref.quote: When the number of moles of reactants and products in balanced chemical equations are equal

blocks.prompt: 49 The unit of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is:
blocks.explanation: (mol dm⁻³)²/[(mol dm⁻³)(mol dm⁻³)³] = 1/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻² dm⁶ (8.8.2).

book_ref.quote: In the synthesis of NH₃ by Haber’s process, the units of reactants and products are not cancelled.

blocks.prompt: 50 The unit of Kc for 2N₂O₅(g) ⇌ 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g) is:
blocks.explanation: Kc = [NO₂]⁴[O₂]/[N₂O₅]² has (mol dm⁻³)⁵/(mol dm⁻³)² = (mol dm⁻³)³ = mol³ dm⁻⁹ (8.8.2).

book_ref.quote: When the number of moles are unequal, then value of equilibrium constant depend upon the units

blocks.prompt: 51 Which reaction has an equilibrium constant Kc with no units?
blocks.explanation: In H₂O + CO ⇌ H₂ + CO₂, 2 mol of reactants give 2 mol of products, so the units cancel (8.8.2).

book_ref.quote: The ester formation reaction happens in solution state

blocks.prompt: 52 For the general reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the power of [A] in the Kc expression is:
blocks.explanation: Each concentration is raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation, so [A] carries the power a (8.8).

book_ref.quote: Then Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ

blocks.prompt: 53 How many different types of quantities may be used to calculate the equilibrium constants of a reversible reaction?
blocks.explanation: Concentrations, partial pressures, numbers of moles and mole fractions give Kc, Kp, Kn and Kx (8.9).

book_ref.quote: There are four different types of quantities which may be used to calculate the equilibrium constants

blocks.prompt: 54 The equilibrium constant written in terms of partial pressures of gases is:
blocks.explanation: When concentrations are expressed as partial pressures, the constant is Kp (8.9).

book_ref.quote: When the concentrations are expressed in terms of partial pressures (p) for gaseous reactants and products

blocks.prompt: 55 Kx is the equilibrium constant expressed in terms of:
blocks.explanation: Kx uses mole fractions (X) of reactants and products (8.9).

book_ref.quote: When the concentrations are expressed in terms of mole fractions, (X) then

blocks.prompt: 56 In Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, Δn for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) is:
blocks.explanation: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants = 2 − 3 = −1 (8.9).

book_ref.quote: Δn = Difference of number of moles of products and reactants in the balanced chemical equation

blocks.prompt: 57 For which reaction is Δn = +3?

book_ref.quote: Δn = Difference of number of moles of products and reactants in the balanced chemical equation

blocks.prompt: 58 Kp = Kc = Kx = Kn when:
blocks.explanation: If the moles of reactants and products in the balanced equation are equal, Δn = 0 and all the constants are equal (8.9).

book_ref.quote: Hence, whichever concentration units are used, the equilibrium constants are same.

blocks.prompt: 59 The relation between Kp and Kx is:
blocks.explanation: Equation (6) of section 8.9: Kp = Kx(P)^Δn, where P is the pressure of the system (8.9).

book_ref.quote: The relationships between these equilibrium constants are as follows:

blocks.prompt: 60 The correct relation between Kp and Kn is:
blocks.explanation: Each partial pressure is p = (n/N) × P, so Kp = Kn(P/N)^Δn (8.9, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Each partial pressure is p = (n / N) × P, so equation (7) should be Kp = Kn (P/N)^Δn.

blocks.prompt: 61 For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), Kc = 0.10 at 500 K. Using R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, Kp is about:

book_ref.quote: The formula for conversion of Kc to Kp is, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn

blocks.prompt: 62 For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), Kc = 7.7 × 10⁻⁵ at 273 K. With R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, Kp is about:

book_ref.quote: The formula for conversion of Kc to Kp is, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn

blocks.prompt: 63 For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) the equilibrium partial pressures are SO₂ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, O₂ = 8.0 × 10⁵ Pa and SO₃ = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Kp is:

book_ref.quote: In the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) the equilibrium partial pressures at constant temperature

blocks.prompt: 64 For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at 773 K (RT = 63.5), Kp compared with Kc is:
blocks.explanation: Δn = −2, so Kp = Kc/(RT)²; with RT = 63.5 the value of Kp is less than Kc (8.9).

book_ref.quote: So, the value of Kp is less than Kc.

blocks.prompt: 65 In the relation Kp = Kx(P)^Δn, the symbol P stands for:

options.text: partial pressure of the product only

blocks.explanation: In the list of symbols, P = pressure of the system (8.9).

book_ref.quote: The relationships between these equilibrium constants are as follows:

blocks.text: 8.10 Position of equilibrium and reaction conditions

blocks.prompt: 66 The position of equilibrium refers to:

options.text: the relative amounts of products and reactants in the equilibrium mixture
the place where the vessel is kept
the time taken to reach equilibrium
the speed of the forward reaction only

blocks.explanation: Position of equilibrium means the relative amounts of products and reactants present in an equilibrium mixture (8.10).

book_ref.quote: relative amounts of products and reactants present in an equilibrium mixture

blocks.prompt: 67 If the concentration of products in an equilibrium mixture increases relative to the reactants, the position of equilibrium has shifted:
blocks.explanation: When products increase relative to reactants, the equilibrium has shifted to the right, towards the products (8.10, book correction).

book_ref.quote: the position of equilibrium has shifted to the right (towards the products)

blocks.prompt: 68 According to Le Chatelier's principle, when a system in equilibrium is disturbed, it behaves so as to:

options.text: nullify the effect of the disturbance

blocks.explanation: If a system in equilibrium is disturbed, it behaves in such a way as to nullify the effect of that disturbance (8.11).

book_ref.quote: it behaves in such a way as to nullify the effect of that disturbance

blocks.prompt: 69 Henry-Louis Le Chatelier was a:
blocks.explanation: Le Chatelier (1850-1936) was a French chemist (8.11).

book_ref.quote: (1850-1936) A French chemist of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

blocks.prompt: 70 Which of the following is NOT one of the effects studied as applications of Le Chatelier's principle in this chapter?

options.text: effect of the colour of the vessel

blocks.explanation: The applications listed are the effects of concentration, pressure, temperature and catalyst (8.11.1).

book_ref.quote: Some of the most common applications of this principle with reference to certain physical

blocks.text: 8.12 The effect of a change of concentration

blocks.prompt: 71 When water is added to a BiCl₃ solution, the solution becomes cloudy because of the formation of:
blocks.explanation: BiCl₃ reacts with water to give the white insoluble compound BiOCl, which makes the solution cloudy (8.12).

book_ref.quote: BiCl₃ reacts with water to give a white insoluble compound, BiOCl.

blocks.prompt: 72 The correct equilibrium constant expression for BiCl₃ + H₂O ⇌ BiOCl + 2HCl is:
blocks.explanation: BiOCl is an insoluble solid, and a pure solid is not written in Kc: Kc = [HCl]²/[BiCl₃][H₂O] (8.12, book correction).

book_ref.quote: a pure solid is not included in the equilibrium constant expression, so [BiOCl] is left out

blocks.prompt: 73 If a few moles of BiCl₃ are added to the BiCl₃ hydrolysis equilibrium, the reaction:

options.text: is pushed in the forward direction

blocks.explanation: Adding BiCl₃ (a reactant) disturbs the equilibrium; more BiOCl and HCl form, i.e. the forward direction (8.12).

book_ref.quote: If a few moles of BiCl₃ are added at equilibrium, the reaction is pushed to the forward direction.

blocks.prompt: 74 In BiCl₃ + H₂O ⇌ BiOCl + 2HCl, which addition shifts the equilibrium in the reverse direction?
blocks.explanation: Adding HCl, a product in solution, moves the reaction backwards; adding solid BiOCl does not shift it (8.12, book correction).

book_ref.quote: BiOCl is a solid, so adding a little more BiOCl does not shift the equilibrium; only adding HCl does.

blocks.prompt: 75 If some BiCl₃ is removed from the BiCl₃ hydrolysis equilibrium, the reaction moves:
blocks.explanation: Removing BiCl₃ makes the reaction move in the reverse direction to compensate; Kc stays constant (8.12).

book_ref.quote: If a certain amount of BiCl₃ is removed at equilibrium stage, the reaction will move in the reverse direction

blocks.prompt: 76 When the concentration of a reactant in an equilibrium mixture is changed at constant temperature:

options.text: both the position and Kc change
Kc changes but the position does not
the position changes but Kc stays constant

blocks.explanation: Adding or removing a substance changes the equilibrium position, but Kc remains constant (8.12).

book_ref.quote: Kc remains constant, but equilibrium position has changed.

blocks.prompt: 77 How many possibilities does the book give for changing the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium?
blocks.explanation: There are four possibilities: adding or removing a reactant, and adding or removing a product (8.12).

book_ref.quote: There are four possibilities for the change in concentrations of reactants and products.

blocks.text: 8.13 The effect of a change in pressure or volume

blocks.prompt: 78 The effect of a change in pressure on an equilibrium does not apply when:

options.text: the gaseous moles of reactants and products are unequal
the system has no gaseous components

blocks.explanation: Pressure has no effect when the system has no gaseous components, or when gaseous moles of reactants and products are equal (8.13).

book_ref.quote: The system does not involve gaseous components.

blocks.prompt: 79 A change of pressure will shift the position of which equilibrium?
blocks.explanation: Only the SO₃ equilibrium has unequal gaseous moles (3 → 2); the others have equal gas moles or no gases (8.13).

book_ref.quote: This effect can only be discussed if the gaseous moles of reactants and products are unequal.

blocks.prompt: 80 If the pressure on the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is increased:
blocks.explanation: The forward reaction decreases the number of moles and the volume, so higher pressure shifts it forward: more NH₃ (8.13).

book_ref.quote: So, if pressure is increased at equilibrium, more ammonia is produced.

blocks.prompt: 81 If the volume of the vessel containing N₂, H₂ and NH₃ at equilibrium is increased, the reaction:
blocks.explanation: Lower pressure (larger volume) moves the reaction to the side that occupies greater volume; ammonia synthesis shifts backwards (8.13).

book_ref.quote: the reaction will move to that side, where the reaction occupies greater volume

blocks.prompt: 82 Pressure has no effect on the gaseous homogeneous equilibrium in which:

options.text: only one gas is a product

blocks.explanation: When the number of moles of reactants and products are equal in a gaseous homogeneous equilibrium, pressure has no effect (8.13).

book_ref.quote: The number of moles of reactants and products are equal in gaseous phase homogeneous equilibrium.

blocks.text: 8.14 The effect of a change in temperature

blocks.prompt: 83 Which factor changes the value of the equilibrium constant Kc?
blocks.explanation: Temperature is the only factor that also affects the value of Kc (8.14).

book_ref.quote: Temperature is the only factor that also affects the value of equilibrium constant (Kc).

blocks.prompt: 84 For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, an increase in temperature:
blocks.explanation: For an exothermic reaction, adding heat favours the reverse reaction (8.14).

book_ref.quote: For an exothermic reaction, an increase in temperature (adding heat) favours the reverse reaction.

blocks.prompt: 85 For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH° = −198 kJ, Kc at 298 K is 1 × 10²⁶ and at 1000 K is 2.8 × 10². This shows that raising the temperature:

options.text: decreases Kc and the yield of SO₃
increases Kc and the yield of SO₃

blocks.explanation: The reaction is exothermic; higher temperature shifts it to the left, so Kc and SO₃ decrease (8.14).

book_ref.quote: Kc for this reaction is 2.8 × 10² at 1000 K; whereas, at 298 K the value of Kc is 1 × 10²⁶.

blocks.prompt: 86 For the exothermic formation of SO₃, a decrease in temperature:

options.text: shifts it from right to left and decreases Kc
shifts the reaction from left to right and increases Kc
shifts it to the right but decreases Kc
